open_obligations: Check whether amplification, shown in algorithmic environments, carries over to Amodei et al.'s cleaning-robot example, where human checks may have to be infrequent.
Check whether a hard-coded decomposer can stand in for the expensive human check in Amodei et al.'s setting.

Note that the reported saving is in examples for learning decompositions on algorithmic tasks, and that Christiano et al. expect the sample complexity to be much larger for realistic tasks; check whether amplification still reduces the number of expensive human checks in Amodei et al.'s setting.
in.other_title: Iterated Amplification: training signal built by combining solutions to easier subproblems
in.rationale: Amodei et al. ask how to ensure an agent respects aspects of an objective too expensive to evaluate often during training. Christiano et al. propose Iterated Amplification, which builds a training signal for problems too complicated for a human to evaluate by combining solutions to easier subproblems, and present results in algorithmic environments. There, amplification needed tens of thousands of examples to learn the decompositions, while supervised learning needed tens of millions, which they say would be a prohibitive cost if an external expert provided the examples.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how to train when human evaluation is too expensive to do frequently (Amodei et al.) or too complicated to do directly (Christiano et al.), via a training signal built from easier subproblems

open_obligations: Check whether Leike et al. test recursive reward modeling experimentally; the cited passage only describes the procedure.
Check whether assistance reduces the frequency of expensive user checks or only their difficulty.
Check whether the sub-problems the user carves off need to cover the whole evaluation, and how that is ensured.
in.other_title: Recursive reward modeling: agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating agent A(k)
in.rationale: Amodei et al. ask how an agent can respect objectives too expensive to evaluate frequently. Leike et al. propose recursive reward modeling, in which agent A(k-1) helps the user evaluate outcomes when training A(k), e.g. by summarising data or solving carved-off sub-problems; the cited passage presents it as a procedure to imagine ('Imagine repeating the following procedure') and reports no results.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how to train agents on objectives users cannot cheaply evaluate, via reward modeling with agent assistance

text: Using a cleaning-robot example, the authors pose the question of how to efficiently ensure that the robot respects aspects of the objective too expensive to evaluate frequently during training, e.g. discarding candy wrappers but setting aside cellphones. Asking humans whether they lost anything can serve as a check but may have to be infrequent, so the robot must do the right thing despite limited information.
title: Scalable oversight question: respecting aspects of the objective too costly to evaluate frequently during training
